The Board of Directors, in their meeting held on 03rd November, 2025, had declared 1st Interim Dividend of ₹4.50 per equity share of ₹10/- each i.e. @45% of the paid-up equity share capital for financial year (FY) 2025-26 and was paid on 01st December, 2025. The Board of Directors in their meeting held on 30th January, 2026 had declared 2nd Interim Dividend of ₹3.25 per equity share of ₹10/- each i.e. @32.50% of the paid-up equity share capital for the financial year (FY) 2025-26 and was paid on 27th February, 2026. Members who have not received the Dividend may approach KFin Technologies Limited, Registrar and Share Transfer Agent (“KFINTECH” / “RTA”) of the Company for claiming dividend. The Board of Directors in their meeting held on 15th May, 2026 had recommended Final Dividend of ₹1.25 per equity share (i.e.@12.5% on the paid-up equity share capital) for the financial year 2025-26. The Record Date for determining the entitlement of the Members for the Final Dividend is Thursday, 13th August, 2026. If the Final Dividend, as recommended by the Board of Directors, is approved at the AGM, such dividend, subject to deduction of tax at source, will be paid on or before Wednesday, 16th September, 2026.

Business Portfolio
Power Transmission
POWERGRID is India’s leading Company in bulk power transmission, operating an extensive network of Extra High Voltage AC and High Voltage DC systems.
Through the development of high-capacity inter-State and intra-State transmission systems, POWERGRID continues to strengthen grid stability, enhance connectivity and facilitate seamless regional integration. The Company has been playing a pivotal role in energy transition goals of the country by integrating various renewable energy zones into the national grid. The Company is also the executing agency for cross-border interconnections with neighbouring countries.
POWERGRID uses technologies such as 765 kV and 400 kV EHVAC substations, LCC and VSC based HVDC links and advanced reactive power management systems that include SVCs and STATCOMs creating a meshed grid that can reliably transmit bulk power.
Telecom

Telecom
Through its wholly owned subsidiary, POWERGRID Teleservices Limited (PowerTel), the Company has established a strong presence in the telecommunications sector by leveraging its nationwide optical ground wire (OPGW) network. PowerTel is the only telecom service provider to have pan India overhead optic fibre network on Extra High Voltage Transmission Lines and is now expanding its services to Data Centre business.
Consultancy
POWERGRID offers specialised consultancy services to domestic and international clients, drawing upon its deep expertise in power transmission, sub- transmission, distribution management, load dispatch and communication systems. Leveraging its tech-managerial prowess, POWERGRID has expanded its global footprint with consultancy services delivered to over 150 domestic and 25 international clients across 25 countries.
Other Businesses
POWERGRID through its wholly owned subsidiary, POWEGRID Energy Services Limited (PESL), has recently broadened its businesses portfolio and taken up pilot projects in emerging sectors such as solar power generation, smart metering solutions, Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and green hydrogen production, aligning with the evolving energy landscape and future growth opportunities.

Reliability Centred Maintenance

Reliability Centred Maintenance
Leveraging modern technologies-such as drones, LiDAR mapping, mechanisation, modular construction and digital tracking platforms-significantly accelerates project execution, improve safety, reduce costs and drive operational excellence.
POWERGRID has adopted a Reliability-Centred Maintenance (RCM) framework, transitioning from time- based maintenance to a ‘condition-based and risk-based’ approach to enhance asset reliability and operational efficiency.
Asset Coverage: Applied across critical assets, including transformers, reactors, circuit breakers and transmission lines.
Data-Driven Maintenance: Utilises key condition indicators such as Dissolved Gas Analysis, oil quality parameters, thermography, SCADA alarms, SF6 monitoring, inspection records and loading patterns.
Risk-Based Prioritisation: Maintenance activities are prioritised based on asset health, criticality and risk scores, enabling timely monitoring, refurbishment or replacement.
Advanced Analytics: Leverages AI/ML and predictive analytics, including image-based defect detection and operational data analysis, to assess the probability and impact of failure.
Outcomes: Enhances asset availability and reliability, reduces outages, extends asset life, lowers lifecycle costs and improves overall maintenance effectiveness.

SF6 Monitoring & Mitigation Measures
SF6 is widely used in electrical substations for its specific properties and constitutes majority of POWERGRID’s Scope 1 emissions due to its high Global Warming Potential (GWP). Recognizing its environmental impact, the Company has implemented a focused SF6 management program aimed at reducing leakages across operations. Key measures include sensitization of employees on the climate impacts of SF6, specialized training programs, strengthened inventory management practices and robust leakage detection and rectification systems. As a result of these initiatives, SF6 leakage is showing a declining trend from 0.15% in 2021-22 to 0.06% in FY 2025-26. In absolute terms this translates to reduction of SF6 leakage from 4,409 kg to 2,481 kg, which is equivalent to an emission saving of 46,849 tCO2e. Water Management

Biodiversity and Ecological Stewardship

Biodiversity and Ecological Stewardship
POWERGRID follows a structured approach to environmental and social management across its projects and operations, guided by the principles of Avoidance, Minimization and Mitigation. These principles are embedded within the Company’s Environmental and Social Policy and Procedures (ESPP) framework and are applied throughout the project lifecycle to reduce ecological disturbance, minimize social impacts and support long-term environmental sustainability.
Integrating Biodiversity considerations into Project Planning
POWERGRID recognizes biodiversity conservation as an integral part of its project planning and operational approach. The Company seeks to minimize impacts on forests, wildlife habitats and other ecologically sensitive areas right from the project conceptualization stage and throughout the project lifecycle. Biodiversity considerations are integrated into route selection and project design to reduce disturbance to natural ecosystems while ensuring reliable transmission infrastructure development.
Avoidance

Avoidance
POWERGRID prioritises the avoidance of environmental and social impacts by carefully evaluating alternative routes and sites during project planning. Efforts are made to avoid ecologically and socially sensitive areas, including forests, wildlife habitats, residential zones, religious sites and culturally significant locations, wherever feasible.
Wherever feasible, transmission line routes are optimized to avoid forests, wildlife sanctuaries, national parks, wetlands, Ramsar sites, important bird areas, elephant corridors and other ecologically significant landscapes. In cases where forest involvement becomes unavoidable due to terrain or geographical constraints, vegetation clearance is restricted to the minimum required area beneath conductors, allowing natural revegetation across most portions of the Right of Way (RoW).
Minimization
Further, in order to minimise the impacts of transmission lines passing through forest/ protected areas, the actual tree felling is limited to two strips of 3-10 meters depending upon the voltage level and tower configuration. Additionally regeneration of vegetation is allowed in one of the strips and only one strip is completely kept clear of vegetation for operation and maintenance purpose.

In situations where complete avoidance is not possible due to terrain, technical, or geographical constraints, the Company undertakes measures to minimize impacts through route optimization and careful placement of transmission lines and substations. This helps reduce the extent of involvement of forest and wildlife areas while limiting the overall environmental footprint of projects.
Mitigation
To address residual environmental and social impacts arising from project activities, POWERGRID implements a range of mitigation measures:

implementation of mitigation measures during execution.

land through mutually agreed arrangements for substations, thereby minimizing involuntary land acquisition.

Case Study: Avoidance/Minimization of Ecological Sensitive Areas in NERPSIP
Background

Background
POWERGRID was involved as Project Management Consultant and Implementation Agency in the crucial North Eastern Region Power System Improvement Project (NERPSIP) by Govt of India to strengthen Transmission and Distribution (T&D) system across six North Eastern states—Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Nagaland and Mizoram, which were facing significant bottlenecks in access and availability of reliable power supply. The project entailed construction of approximately 1,400 km of 220/132 kV transmission lines, 34 associated 220/132/66/33 kV substations, 2,051 km of 33 kV distribution lines and 85 numbers of 33/11 kV substations, along with augmentation/extension of existing substations and reconductoring works. The project was jointly funded by Govt of India and the World Bank.
E&S Safeguard Challenges

E&S Safeguard Challenges
The North Eastern Region (NER), a recognized global biodiversity hotspot, hosts over 30–50% of India’s biodiversity with high endemism and >60% forest cover across most states, indicating significant environmental sensitivity. Accordingly, the World Bank categorized the project as High Risk (Category “A”), which essentially means that the project involves potential significant and complex environmental and social impacts. Given the linear and extensive nature of transmission & distribution lines coupled with presence of dense forest/wildlife cover of these states, complete avoidance of ecologically sensitive areas is often not feasible, resulting in very high estimated forest/wildlife involvement in the initial Detailed Project Report (DPR).
POWERGRID efforts to address the Challenges

POWERGRID efforts to address the Challenges
POWERGRID, leveraging its extensive experience in executing transmission projects across the country and its proven track record in complying with Environmental and Social (E&S) safeguards of multilateral institutions, including the World Bank, has taken up the challenge. By employing a balanced application of the mitigation hierarchy (avoid–minimize–mitigate), study of multiple line routes involving modern survey techniques and conducting extensive consultations with public, community leaders and forest/ revenue officials attempted to ensure avoidance and minimization of Forest/wildlife areas.
The results obtained through this extensive safeguard process were extremely encouraging, including complete avoidance of forest/wildlife areas in Assam and Nagaland and substantial reduction in other states. Consequently, the overall forest/wildlife involvement was reduced to 10.63%, representing a major decline from DPR estimates (41.82%). This optimization not only led to conservation of approximately 1388 ha. of forest resources but also yielded cost savings of more than ₹150 crore by reducing liabilities towards forest diversion and compensatory measures.

Project Overview
The POWERGRID Vidyalakshmi Scholarship is a Merit-Cum-Means (MCM) scholarship initiative aimed at supporting economically weaker students pursuing B.Tech programmes at premier technical institutions across India. Launched in 2022 with Indian Institute of Technology Madras as the nodal institution, the programme seeks to improve access to higher technical education by reducing financial barriers for deserving students.

POWERGRID, in partnership with the National Foundation for Communal Harmony under the Ministry of Home Affairs, has been supporting education of children affected by communal, caste, ethnic, terrorist and naxal violence since 2014. The initiative aims to provide financial assistance for education and rehabilitation of children from economically weaker families who lost parents or primary bread earners due to violence. Financial support is provided annually in advance for students pursuing education from school level up to graduation, post-graduation and professional courses such as MBBS, MBA, M.Tech, MCA, B.Tech, B.Ed, BBA, Nursing and LLB.
The scholarship programme follows a self-sustaining endowment model wherein the corpus funds are strategically invested and the generated interest is utilized to finance annual scholarships. This approach supports long-term financial sustainability and continuity of the programme.
The project primarily supports children from Manipur, Assam and Chhattisgarh, including remote and violence - affected regions. Assistance is extended to children from families with annual income below ₹2 lakh.

Vendor Screening and Selection
Ensuring Transparent Engagement and Responsive Grievance Resolution
Vendor selection at POWERGRID is based on transparent and objective evaluation processes covering technical capability, manufacturing infrastructure, product quality, testing facilities, delivery performance and competitive pricing.
During the project planning stage, both formal and informal, public consultations are conducted to gather community insights on sensitive local sites, alongside published newspaper notices in local languages to ensure full transparency and address public feedback before construction begins
POWERGRID undertakes comprehensive screening and assessment potential suppliers through structured evaluation mechanisms and online vendor registration systems. Suppliers are assessed on criteria covering statutory compliance, quality systems, manufacturing capability, safety practices, environmental management and social accountability standards such as prohibiting child labour, non-discrimination, adherence to minimum wage requirements and worker welfare practices.

Public Grievance Redress Mechanism
Supplier Code of Conduct and Sustainability Integration

Supplier Code of Conduct and Sustainability Integration
To further smoothen the relationship with community, the Company has developed an effective Grievance Redress Mechanism to resolve any leftover grievance of community/public. The GRM has two tiers, the first being Project/Substation level Grievance Redress Committee (GRC) and the second being the Corporate Level GRC chaired by the Director (Projects) of the Company. All written and verbal complaints received by Project level GRC are to be resolved within 20 days of receipt of complaint. If the complainant is not satisfied with the outcome of the project level GRC, he/she can approach the Corporate Level GRC, which in turn has to resolve the complaint/grievance within 45 days.
POWERGRID's Supplier Code of Conduct sets expectations on ethics, human rights, workplace safety, environmental management and statutory compliance. The Company also conducts supplier engagement and sensitization programmes to strengthen sustainability awareness and encourage alignment with POWERGRID's sustainability objectives and BRSR Core requirements.

Your Company had incorporated a wholly-owned subsidiary, Central Transmission Utility of lndia Limited (CTUIL), in December 2020 for carrying out statutory functions of central transmission utility as per Section 38 of the Electricity Act 2003 and other functions as assigned by Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC). 2.1 Global Power Sector
The global power sector is undergoing a fundamental shift from a centralised, fossil-fuel-based model to a decentralised, digitised and decarbonised ecosystem. The sector is witnessing a surge in electricity demand, driven by the rapid expansion of AI-enabled data centres, the transition to low carbon energy sources, and the growing requirements for advanced cooling solutions. This trend is further reinforced by a global manufacturing revival, which requires power grids to deliver reliable and scalable energy.
Key Trends and Developments

Key Trends and Developments
IEA's Electricity 2026 report highlights that transmission networks and grid modernisation will play a pivotal role in enabling reliable, resilient and sustainable electricity systems. Key global trends include:
● Electrification and Demand Growth: Global electricity demand grew by 3.0% in 2025, following a 4.4% increase in 2024 and an average growth of 2.7% during 2010–2023. Demand is projected to rise at an average 3.6% annually during 2026–2030, growing at least 2.5 times faster than overall energy demand, driven by industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centres. Annual demand growth over the next five years is expected to be 50% higher than the previous decade’s average, with emerging economies accounting for nearly 80% of additional consumption, led by India and Southeast Asia.
● Renewable Energy Expansion: On the supply side, renewable energy continues to lead global capacity additions. Renewables and nuclear together are expected to account for about half of global electricity generation by 2030. In percentage terms, renewable generation is forecast to rise at an annual rate of 8% per year. Renewable output is forecast to grow by about 1,000 TWh annually through 2030, with solar PV alone accounting for over 600 TWh of that annual growth.

● Decarbonization and Emissions: The transition to low-carbon energy sources is reshaping global generation portfolios. The continued decline in carbon dioxide emissions from the power sector is being accelerated by increased use of renewables and advances in energy efficiency.
● System Reliability and Resilience: As power systems integrate higher shares of renewable energy and meet rapidly growing electricity demand, resilient transmission networks have become indispensable.

Right of Way (RoW) Constraints
Securing Right of Way (RoW) for transmission lines continues to be one of the key challenges in project execution. Increasing urbanisation, expanding infrastructure such as highways, railways, pipelines and communication networks, and competing land-use requirements have progressively reduced the availability of suitable transmission corridors. The challenge is particularly acute in renewable energy-rich states, where large transmission corridors must be developed while balancing environmental considerations, forest clearances, wildlife sensitivities and community concerns.
The Company addresses supply-chain constraints through strategic vendor development, diversification of supplier base and long-term procurement planning including bulk procurement. Critical spares planning for key equipment categories ensures operational continuity. POWERGRID has also been actively supporting indigenous manufacturing capability development for high-technology equipment.

An amount of ₹ 3487.50 Crore from bond issue has been recognised as Grant in aid in earlier year. * Details of advances to related parties are provided in Note 55. ** The Central Commission vide order dated 06/04/2015 in Petition No.127/2012 had directed that 80% of the acquisition price incurred by the Company for Vemagiri Transmission Company Limited (VTSL) shall be reimbursed by the Long-Term Transmission Customers (LTTCs) and balance 20% along with the expenditure incurred by VTSL from the date of acquisition till the liquidation of the company shall be borne by the Company. Aggrieved thereby, the Company filed a Review Petition, wherein Central Commission, vide order dated 20.10.2016, observed that there were sufficient grounds to reconsider the Company’s liability towards the 20% acquisition cost. Accordingly, Central Commission directed that the issue of the Company’s liability shall be decided afresh, after the final disposal of the appeals pending before the Hon’ble Tribunal for Electricity. Before the Hon’ble Tribunal, the matter underwent multiple hearings between 2020 and 2024. Hon’ble Tribunal finally pronounced the judgment on 22.07.2025 wherein it held that Company is not liable to bear the acquisition cost paid by it under compelling circumstances and that such acquisition cost is required to be borne by RECPDCL (erstwhile RECPTCL). Accordingly, Hon’ble Tribunal remanded matter back to Central Commission with a direction to take appropriate measures in accordance with law to give effect to the same.

Aggrieved by the said judgment, RECPDCL filed Civil Appeal Nos. 11011–11013 of 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, by order dated 10.10.2025, dismissed the appeals and upheld the Hon’ble Tribunal’s order dated 22.07.2025, observing that no ground was made out to interfere with the remand issued on the principles of fairness and restitution. Thereafter, the matter was heard by the Central Commission in remand proceedings, wherein Company submitted that it was entitled for principal acquisition cost Rs. 18.27 crores , carrying cost amounting to Rs. 31.52 crores calculated for period of date of acquisition, i.e., 18.04.2012 to 31.12.2025, operational cost relating to SPV expenditure amounting to Rs. 1.21 crores and legal expenditure incurred. However, the Central Commission, vide its order dated 07.03.2026, held that the direction in the Hon’ble Tribunal judgment being limited to adjustment of the acquisition cost paid by Company, it was impermissible to consider Company’s claim towards SPV expenditure, carrying cost and litigation costs incurred by Company. Accordingly, it directed RECPDCL to pay only an amount of Rs. 18.27 crores to Company towards the acquisition cost of the SPV within thirty days from the date of the order. In pursuance of the said order dated 07.03.2026, RECPDCL paid the acquisition cost of Rs.18.27 crores to Company. Company has received the said amount towards SPV acquisition cost on 21.04.2026. Accordingly, the provision for doubtful advances of Rs 18.27 crore has been reversed during the year. In view of the disallowance, the Company filed an Appeal before the Hon’ble Tribunal on 21.04.2026 vide DFR No. 196 of 2026 on limited grounds confined to the carrying cost, operational cost towards SPV expenditure, and litigation expenses.

CERC Sharing regulation allow payment against monthly bills towards transmission charges within due date i.e., 45 days from the date of presentation of the bill and levy of surcharge on delayed payment beyond 45 days. However, in order to improve the cash flows of transmission licensee, CTUIL provides a graded rebate for payments made within 45 days. If a DIC fails to pay any bill or part thereof by the Due Date, the Central Transmission Utility (CTUIL) may encash the Letter of Credit provided by the DIC and utilise the same towards the amount of the bill or part thereof that is overdue plus Late Payment Surcharge, if applicable.

(B) LIQUIDITY RISK
The Company is exposed to currency risk mainly in respect of foreign currency denominated loans and borrowings and procurement of goods and services whose purchase consideration is denominated in foreign currency. Transmission tariff is regulated by the CERC. According to the CERC tariff regulations for the block 2024-29 the Company may hedge foreign exchange exposure in respect of the interest on foreign currency loan and repayment of foreign loan acquired for the transmission system, in part or full in its discretion and recover the cost of hedging of foreign exchange rate variation corresponding to the normative foreign debt, in the relevant year.

Liquidity risk management implies maintaining sufficient cash and marketable securities and the availability of funding through an adequate amount of committed credit facilities to meet obligations when due. The Company monitors its risk of a shortage of funds using a liquidity planning tool. The Company has access to a variety of sources of funding such as commercial paper, bank loans, bonds and external commercial borrowings and retains flexibility in funding by maintaining availability under committed credit lines.
Management monitors rolling forecasts of the Company’s liquidity position comprising the undrawn borrowing facilities below and cash and cash equivalents on the basis of expected cash flows.
If hedging of the foreign exchange exposure is not undertaken, the extra rupee liability towards interest payment and loan repayment corresponding to the normative foreign currency loan in the relevant year is permissible to be recovered as part of transmission tariff provided it is not attributable to the generating Company or the transmission licensee or its suppliers or contractors. In respect of goods and services procured for Capital Investment, the exchange rate variation is part of the project cost, for determination of transmission tariff. The currency risk in respect of goods and services procured for operation activities is not significant.

The Company has Post-Retirement Medical Facility (PRMF), under which retired employees and their eligible dependents are provided medical facilities in the empanelled/non-empanelled hospitals. Equity Method

Equity Method
Initial Recognition and Measurement
Under the equity method of accounting, the investments are initially recognised at cost and adjusted thereafter to recognise the Group’s share of the post – acquisition profits or losses of the investee company in Statement of Profit and Loss, and the Group’s share of other comprehensive income of the investee Company in other comprehensive income. (i) Trade Receivables and Contract Assets
The Group primarily provides transmission facilities to inter-state transmission service customers (DICs) comprising mainly state utilities owned by State Governments and the main revenue is from transmission charges. CERC (Sharing of Inter-State Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2020 (“CERC Sharing Regulations”) allow payment against monthly bills towards transmission charges within due date i.e., 45 days from the date of presentation of the bill and levy of surcharge on delayed payment beyond 45 days. However, in order to improve the cash flows of group, a graded rebate is provided for payments made within 45 days. If a DIC fails to pay any bill or part thereof by the Due Date, the Central Transmission Utility (CTU) may encash the Letter of Credit provided by the DIC and utilise the same towards the amount of the bill or part thereof that is overdue plus Late Payment Surcharge, if applicable.

The scheme is funded by the Company and is managed by a separate trust. The liability for the same is recognised on the basis of actuarial valuation on annual basis on the Balance Sheet date.

II. POWERGRID Employee family rehabilitation scheme
(₹ in crore)
The Group has introduced POWERGRID Employees Family Economic Rehabilitation Scheme on 24 June 2017. The Objective of the scheme is to provide monetary assistance and support to an employee in case of his/ her permanent total disablement and to his/her family in case of death while in service. The beneficiary would be entitled to monthly payment equivalent to the employee’s 50% of one month pay last drawn provided the beneficiary deposits with the Group an amount equal to PF (excluding VPF) balance, Gratuity amount and Group Insurance (EDLI) amount. Such monthly payment would continue till the normal notional date on which the employee concerned would have attained the age of superannuation had the employee continued in the service of the Group. The scheme is optional. Provision for POWERGRID Employees Family Economic Rehabilitation Scheme amounting to ₹3.31crore (Previous Year ₹4.45crore) for the year has been made during the year based on actuarial valuation.

Opinion
We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (hereinafter referred to as the “Holding Company”), and its subsidiaries (The Holding Company and its subsidiaries together referred to as “the Group”), and its joint ventures, which comprise the consolidated Balance Sheet as at March 31, 2026, the Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss, the Statement of Other Comprehensive Income, the Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity and the Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows for the year ended, and notes to the consolidated financial statement, including material accounting policies and other explanatory information (hereinafter referred to as “the Consolidated Financial Statements”).

2 Reassessment of Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) and Deferred Tax Assets relating to Minimum Alternate Tax (“MAT”) credit entitlement

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting With Reference to Consolidated Financial Statements
A Company's internal financial control over financial reporting with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal financial control over financial reporting with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements includes those policies and procedures that:
i. pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company;

Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting With Reference to Consolidated Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls over financial reporting with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. economic growth, imminent increase in the share of electricity in the energy basket, large-scale renewable energy integration, and the Government's vision to achieve net zero ambition.
